findings.title: Release workflow grants write/OIDC permissions to jobs that execute unpinned registry code
findings.description: The workflow sets top-level contents:write and id-token:write, so jobs inherit release-class permissions unless overridden. Several inherited-permission jobs execute package-manager-fetched code: npx @cyclonedx/cdxgen@10 in SBOM jobs and pip install build hatchling in the SDK packaging job. A compromised registry package or mutable major version can execute inside a release workflow with unnecessary token/OIDC surface.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker compromises @cyclonedx/cdxgen major tag resolution or a transitive package, or compromises build/hatchling resolution. 2. Maintainer pushes a v* tag or manually dispatches release-attestation. 3. Malicious install/runtime code executes in a job inheriting contents:write/id-token:write and a checkout with persisted credentials. 4. Attacker uses the workflow token/OIDC channel or git credentials to tamper with release artifacts, create repo writes, or mint attestations tied to the trusted workflow identity.
findings.impact: Release pipeline compromise: signed SBOMs or package artifacts can be generated from attacker-controlled code, and unnecessary write/OIDC permissions expand blast radius.
findings.recommendation: Set workflow-level permissions to contents:read only, then grant contents:write/id-token:write only on jobs that actually upload releases, sign with cosign, or publish via trusted publisher. Add persist-credentials:false to checkouts in jobs that never push. Replace npx @cyclonedx/cdxgen@10 with an exact pinned version plus integrity verification or a locked tool install. Install Python build tooling from a checked-in lock/constraints file inside a venv, not unpinned into system Python.

findings.title: Release notify job prints private site repository identity to public workflow logs
findings.description: The workflow comments state that SITE_SYNC_REPO is kept in a repository variable so the private site repository name never appears in public source or git history. The notify step then echoes SITE_REPO and also includes it in failure remediation logs. On a public repository, release workflow logs can expose the private repo name to anyone with log access.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Maintainer configures SITE_SYNC_REPO for the private marketing-site repository. 2. A v* tag release runs the notify job. 3. The job prints the private owner/name in Actions logs. 4. An attacker monitoring public release logs learns the private repo identity and uses it for targeted GitHub phishing, dependency confusion reconnaissance, or workflow-dispatch probing.
findings.impact: Private infrastructure metadata leaks despite the repo's explicit design goal to keep that identity out of public source.
findings.recommendation: Stop printing SITE_REPO and SITE_WORKFLOW values. Log only a masked or hashed target identifier, for example owner/repo hash prefix, and keep failure messages generic. If debugging needs the concrete target, emit it only behind a manual debug flag in a private runner context.
